title: Amorphous urchin-like copper@nanosilica hybrid for efficient CO2 electroreduction to C2+ products
abstract: Currently most of research efforts for selective electrocatalysis CO2 reduction to C2+ products have relied on crystalline Cu-based catalysts; amorphous Cu with abundant low-coordinated atoms holds greater promise for this conversion yet remains relatively underexplored. Here we report an amorphous urchin-like Cu@nanosilica hybrid synthesized by electrostatic coupling Si polyanions with Cu salt in hydrothermal processes. The Cu@nanosilica electrocatalyst displays excellent CO2 electroreduction activity and selectivity with a Faradic efficiency of 70.5% for C2+ product production, and higher stability compared to the crystalline Cu counterpart. The solar-driven CO2 electrolysis yields an energy efficiency of 20% for C2+ product production. Mechanism study reveals that the urchin-like Cu@nanosilica catalyst with amorphous Cu/Cu dispersion enhances CO2 adsorption and activation to facilitate generation of CO2 * and possible CO* intermediates, and suppresses hydrogen evolution concurrently. The combined effects of both aspects promote efficient C2+ product production from CO2 electroreduction. 2021 Science Press and Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Conversion of CO2 into value-added fuels and chemicals through electrochemical reduction processes, coupled with renewable energy sources such as solar or wind, shows great promise to revolve current energy crisis and environment issues [1]. Among various products from electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR), highenergy density C2+ products including hydrocarbons and oxygenates are highly desired. It requires multi-electron reduction of CO2 for their formation involving multiple step hydrogenation and C–C coupling reactions, whereas these processes are difficult to proceed [2–4]. Numerous transition metal and carbon-based electrocatalysts have been investigated toward efficient ECR [5– 9]. Cu, in particular, is the only metal catalyst enabling multielectron ECR with C–C coupling on account of its moderate binding energy with *CO, a pivot intermediate for formation of C2+ hydrocarbons and oxygenates [3,10,11]. Therefore, masses of research efforts have been devoted to the development of Cu electrocatalysts, with most of which focusing on crystalline Cu-based material designs in terms of crystallite sizes [12–14], compositions [15],
structures [16–19], facets [20–24], grain boundaries [20,25,26], and strains [27,28].
In contrast to the intensive research on crystalline Cu, amorphous Cu electrocatalysts have been rarely reported thus far, due probably to their being metastable states and the resultant electrocatalytic instability [29]. Nevertheless, amorphous electrocatalysts with long-range out-of-order atom arrangement generally have abundant surface low-coordinated atoms serving as highly active centers, and additional ‘‘dangling bonds” to increase the reactive sites [29,30]. Therefore, amorphous Cu with stable electrocatalytic properties could be the promising candidates for efficient ECR. To obtain efficient and stable amorphous Cu catalysts, the synthesis to control and fix the atomic and micro structures is the prerequisites. However, most of the synthesis methods developed at present, e.g. composite explosive welding, mechanical alloying, jet molding, arc melting pure metals and laser electro-deposition, hardly involve these considerations [31]. Consequently, the synthetic amorphous catalysts from these methods were typically featured with bulk morphology, jumbo size and small specific surface area [32], unfavorable for ECR. Additionally, many of these synthesis methods require expensive instruments and are timeconsuming [31]. Therefore, development of new facile methods for synthesis of amorphous Cu electrocatalysts with high stability and possible size/structure optimization, would promote their
reserved.
applications in ECR. Electrostatic interaction refers to the attraction between two substances charged oppositely [33,34], e.g. cations and anions, which provides the latent basis for atomically fixing metal ions toward amorphization.
Herein, an amorphous urchin-like Cu@nanosilica hybrid was synthesized by electrostatic coupling and hydrothermal processes. The electrochemical measurements indicated high activity and selectivity of this Cu@nanosilica electrocatalyst for ECR to C2+ products, and higher stability compared to the crystalline Cu counterpart. A Faradic efficiency (FE) of 70.5% and an energy efficiency of 20% for C2+ product production were obtained. Various physical and electrochemical characterizations were conducted to reveal the functionalities of amorphous Cu species and urchin-like morphology, which were further correlated to CO2 adsorption/activation, CO2 * and CO* intermediate formation, and the hydrogen evolution effect. This work demonstrates the electrostatic coupling protocol to fabricate stable amorphous Cu-based catalysts for efficient ECR applications.

sections.heading: 2.1. Chemicals and reagents
sections.text: The chemical reagents used in this work include cupric chloride dehydrate (Aladdin, C119000, 99.95%), ethyl orthosilicate (Aladdin, T110596, 99.99%), potassium bicarbonate (Aladdin, P110487, 99.99%), ammonia, Nafion solution (Dupont), 117 Nafion membrane (Dupont), deionized water (Millipore, 18.2 MX cm) and CO2 gas (99.99%). All chemical reagents were used as received without further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of Cu@nanosilica hybrid
sections.text: For the synthesis, 0.3409 g CuCl2 2H2O was dissolved in 10 mL H2O, then 3 mL ethyl orthosilicate and 1 mL NH3 H2O were added into the complex solution. After violent stirring 15 mins, the mixture solution was immediately transferred into a Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave. Then, the autoclave was maintained at 100 C for 12 h. After cooling to room temperature, the resulting precipitate was collected by filtration, rinsed with amounts of deionized water and frozen dry. The obtained material was placed in porcelain in the center of a quartz tube furnace and heated at 500 C in air atmosphere with a heating rate of 5 C min 1. The final obtained power was denoted as Cu@nanosilica hybrid. For comparison, the Cu@nanosilica hybrid was further suffered from heat treatment at the higher temperature to make Cu agglomeration and crystallization, which was designed as Cu@nanosilica 700, Cu@nanosilica 900, and Cu@nanosilica 1000.

sections.heading: 2.3. Physical characterization
sections.text:
The scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL-6700F) was used to characterize the morphology of the as-prepared materials. The structure and element distribution of the materials were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) at the accelerating voltage of 200 kV. X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) was performed with a Philip Xhilip Pro MPP diffractometer using a Cu Ka (k = 1. 54 Å) radiation source at the scan rate of 1 min 1. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed on a Thermo Scientific Escalab 250 Xi and XPS PEAK software was utilized for the XPS data analysis. The chamber pressure of the equipment was maintained below 3 10 10 mbar in the test, and carbon was used to correct using C 1s binding energy of 285 eV. The surface area of materials was obtained using BET measurements at 77 K (ASAP 2010, Micromeritics), and calculating the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller
(BET) equation. Pore size distribution of the material was acquired from simulation of the N2 sorption isotherms using BJH model.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
Electrochemical measurements were conducted by a threeelectrode system in a CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. The electrochemical cell was separated into anodic and cathodic compartments by a 117 Nafion proton membrane. The current of the ECR was measured by chronoamperometry at the given potential. All electrochemical experiments were performed in the electrolyte with bubbling CO2 gas at 20 mL min 1. All the tested potentials were converted to the potentials versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, according to the equation: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.197 + 0.0 59 pH. For the working electrode preparation, 10 mg of the catalyst (Cu@nanosilica and Cu@nanosilica 1000) was dispersed in 2 mL of isopropyl alcohol with 50 ul of Nafion solution. Then, 50 uL of the ink was dropped on the polished glassy carbon (GC) electrode with a diameter of 12 mm and catalyst loading mass is 0.22 mg cm 2.
For the two-electrode electrolysis and solar cell-driven electrolysis, catalyst was coated on the polished GC with the same loading. The electric source was employed by the electrochemical workstation or a commercial-available polycrystalline silicon solar cell. The silicon solar cell had geometric area of 14.6 cm2, and presented a short circuit current density at 5 mA cm 2, as well as an open circuit potential at 2.0 V.

sections.heading: 2.5. Gas detection
sections.text:
Gas products were generated during ECR and detected by a gas chromatograph (GC, 9700II, FULI).
FE of each gas product was calculated using the following equations:
FEgas ¼ igasitotal 100
igas ¼ Cgas vCO2 N 96485 Cgas: production rate, which was measured from gas chromatograms. vCO2 : CO2 flow rate. N: the number of electrons transferred during product formation, which is 2 for both CO and H2, and 8 and 12 for methane and ethylene, respectively.

sections.heading: 2.6. Liquid detection
sections.text: HCOOH production was detected by ion chromatography (IC), while CH3CH2OH and CH3CH2CH2OH production were detected by liquid chromatography (GC, 9720, FULI).

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The synthetic route for the targeted Cu@nanosilica hybrid catalyst was illustrated in Fig. 1, which involves the electrostatic adsorption between Cu and Si precursors in hydrothermal reactions and the pyrolysis processes. Tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) was employed as the silicon source for electrostatically coupling Cu2+ ions. Hydrolysis of TEOS first generated an anionic monomer [SiO(OH)3] [35]. This monomer would polymerize to form dimer and trimer under the catalysis of ammonia, ultimately generating polyanions. One of the typical characteristic is that these polyanions carried negative charge, keeping them stable by electrostatic repulsion in the suspension. More importantly, the Cu2+ ions carrying positive charge in the suspension would be coupled with these polyanions at atomic level. Such coupling was very stable [35].
Besides, this coupling effect reduced the repulsive interaction of these polyanions via neutralizing the charge, causing condensation of the polyanions to form a specific micro-structure. In this way, the silica matrix with a micro-structure was formed with firmly trapping atomic Cu2+, as shown in Fig. 1, which provided the basis for synthesis of amorphous Cu with specific micro-structure in the following pyrolysis. Pyrolysis was used to dehydrate CuSi precursor and fix Cu component. To confirm the Cu and Si components in the as-obtained Cu@nanosilica sample, it was treated with HF and NaOH solution, respectively, with the results photographed in Fig. S1. The pictures indicate that the sample was completely dissolved in HF solution, while some residue remained after NaOH treatment. This result suggested that the synthetic Cu@nanosilica hybrid contained Cu and Si components.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to determine the whole morphology, structure and atom dispersion of the synthetic Cu@nanosilica hybrid. The corresponding SEM images and TEM images, in comparison with the CuSi precursor after hydrothermal reaction, were displayed in Figs. 2 and S3. The SEM images in Figs. 2a and S2 showed that the Cu@nanosilica hybrid had sea urchin morphology, similar with the CuSi polyanion precursor. A more detailed observation by TEM images indicated that the as-formed Cu@nanosilica had the branched micro structure with dense tips, and the mean size of the particles is around 400 nm (see Figs. 2b and S3). On the surface the Cu, Si and O components were uniformly dispersed (see Fig. 2c and S3). The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image in Fig. 2d indicated that there were many branches in the Cu@nanosilica material. These branches contained a lot of cusp and edge domains, which facilitate formation of local electrochemical microenvironment during electrocatalysis. The morphology of Cu@nanosilica 1000 was showed in Fig. S4 for comparison. It can be found that the surface became relatively smooth and the branched micro structure largely disappeared. Also, The Cu mass concentration in Cu@nanosilica and Cu@nanosilica 1000 was measured to be 18.52% and 5.87% by energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Besides, no lattice fringe could be observed in the Cu@nanosilica material, suggesting the amorphous state of Cu. This judgment was also supported by the ambiguous diffuse rings in the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern in Fig. 2e. Additionally, the X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns of the Cu@nanosilica hybrid were presented in Fig. 2f compared to the Cu@nanosilica 1000. No diffraction peak attributed
to Cu component can be observed in Cu@nanosilica hybrid, while there were two CuO peaks (JCPDS no. 80-1916) found in Cu@nanosilica 1000 sample. These results suggested there was crystal Cu in the Cu@nanosilica 1000 sample, while only amorphous Cu existed in the Cu@nanosilica sample. Besides, the broad peak at around 22 indicated the formation of SiO2 in both the samples (JCPDS no. 82-0512). Overall, the Cu@nanosilica hybrid was synthesized from Si polyanions/Cu2+ complex via electrostatic coupling in hydrothermal reactions and pyrolysis processes. The Cu@nanosilica hybrid is consisted of urchin-like morphology with amorphous Cu dispersion, involving numerous surface cusp/edge domains.
To determine the surface element compositions and chemical valences in Cu@nanosilica hybrid, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement was performed. The full scan survey XPS in Fig. S5a indicated the presence of Cu, Si and O elements in the sample. The F signal was also observed because of the addition of Nafion solution. Other peaks attributed to impurity were not found, suggesting the high purity of the obtained Cu@nanosilica hybrid. The Si chemical state was determined by deconvolution of the Si 2p signal, as shown in Fig. S5b. The fitting peak indicated that Si moiety was mainly consisted of Si-O species, suggesting the formation of SiO2 after dehydration. The Cu chemical state will be discussed in the following part. Anyhow, the initial chemical states on Cu catalysts were suggested to be altered in the electrocatalytic ECR [17]. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area of Cu@nanosilica hybrid with urchin-like structure was obtained from nitrogen adsorption–desorption measurement. The isotherm of Cu@nanosilica hybrid displayed the type with mesoporous capillary condensation effect. Its specific surface area was calculated to be 93 m2 g 1 (see Fig. S6a), which was evidently higher than that of the Cu@nanosilica 1000 sample (3.7 m2 g 1). This phenomenon was caused by the abundant micropore and mesopore property stacked by urchin-like structure in the Cu@nanosilica hybrid as shown in Fig. S6b, further providing the basis for tune the local environment in electrocatalysis. In brief, these results indicated that the synthetic Cu@nanosilica hybrid to comprise of Cu, Si and O elements, and its urchin-like structure provided high specific area and possibly tunable local environment for ECR.
To examine ECR performance of the catalyst with evaluating the contribution from urchin-like structure and amorphous Cu, the Cu@nanosilica catalyst loaded on glassy carbon (GC) electrode was electrochemically tested compared to Cu@nanosilica 1000
electrode in a gastight three-electrode system with the 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was first conducted, and the results are shown in Fig. 3a. A quite big difference in currents between CO2- and Ar-saturated electrolytes was found for Cu@nanosilica electrode. At 1.15 V and in the presence of CO2, the current density of 8.332 mA mg 1 was obtained, which was obviously higher than the current (-1.93 mA mg 1) at the same potential but in Ar-saturated solution, suggesting the outstanding activity of the Cu@nanosilica electrode for ECR. Meanwhile, compared with the Cu@nanosilica 1000 electrode, the Cu@nanosilica electrode not only had much higher current density but also exhibited lower onset potential ( 0.7 V) in CO2-saturated solution, suggesting its higher ECR performance than the Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalyst.
Gas chromatograph and ion chromatography were further used to determine the ECR products and activity/selectivity, the results are shown in Fig. 3c–f. Besides H2, there were other six ECR products detected, which were CO, CH4, HCOOH, C2H4, C2H5OH and C3H7OH (Fig. 3c and f). For the Cu@nanosilica electrode, the Faradaic efficiency (FE) of these products at 1.4 V was 6.2%, 3.5%, 11%, 46%, 14.5% and 10%, respectively. The FE at other potentials displayed similar product distribution. Thus, the FE for the overall C2+ products achieved 70.5%, while it even reached 91.2% for C1+ products on the Cu@nanosilica electrode. C2H4 was the main product on the Cu@nanosilica electrode, which was different from that on the Cu@nanosilica 1000 electrode with the main products of CO and H2 (Fig. 3f). The results in Fig. 3d and 3e indicated that Cu@nanosilica electrode had higher C2H4 FE as compared to the Cu@nanosilica 1000 electrode at all tested potentials. As to partial current, the Cu@nanosilica electrode also gave the higher current densities at all tested potentials correspondingly (see Fig. 3b). The highest C2H4 partial current density achieved 11.66 mAmg 1 at 1.4 V on Cu@nanosilica electrode; while for the Cu@nanosilica 1000 electrode, the highest C2H4 partial current density was only
5.304 mA mg 1 at 1.5 V. Overall, the Cu@nanosilica catalyst was demonstrated to show higher ECR performance especially toward C2+ product production, even compared to other reported Cu-based electrocatalysts (see Table S1).
The high ECR efficiency toward C2+ products on the Cu@nanosilica catalyst was inferred to be arisen partially from the amorphous Cu dispersion in the Cu@nanosilica catalyst compared to the Cu@nanosilica 1000. To further confirm this conjecture, the Cu samples annealed at 700 C and 900 C were also examined by ECR test in terms of C2H4 FE. The results in Fig. S7 showed that the Cu@nanosilica 700 and Cu@nanosilica 900 electrodes with crystalline state Cu (form Cu nanoparticles) exhibited lower C2H4 FE compared to the Cu@nanosilica electrode. On the other hand, the H2 FE was only 11.5% at 1.4 V for Cu@nanosilica electrode, probably due to the increasing local pH based on the porous and urchin-like structure. This phenomenonwas also reported byKimet al [17]. To further evidence the pH effect on the Cu@nanosilica electrode, we had further performed control test in CsHCO3 electrolyte. It was proven previously that CsHCO3 electrolytewould cause low local pH during electrolysis due to the high buffer capacity of Cs+ ions, and this trend became significant with the increase of current [36]. The FE of the main products of C2H4 and H2 from hydrogen evolution was determined in CsHCO3 electrolyte and the results are shown in Fig. S8. As expected, the Cu@nanosilica electrode on KHCO3 electrolyte exhibited higher FE for C2H4 and low FE for H2 than that in CsHCO3 electrolyte. These aforesaid results indicated that the excellent ECR activity and selectivity toward C2+ products on the Cu@nanosilica catalyst were arisen from the combined action of amorphous Cu and the urchin-like structure facilitating suppressive hydrogen evolution during electrolysis.
Electrocatalytic durability based on urchin-like structure and amorphous Cu in the Cu@nanosilica catalyst was evaluated by stability study through chronoamperometric measurements at 1.3 V vs. RHE. As shown in Fig. S9, the current of the Cu@nanosilica
electrode kept stable at around 16 mA mg 1, with a slight decay in C2H4 FE and a reservation of 77% after electrolysis for 2 hours. In contrast, although the current of Cu@nanosilica 1000 electrode also kept stable, its reservation for C2H4 FE was only 28% after electrolysis for 2 h. The changes of surface electrochemical and physical properties of the Cu@nanosilica electrode/catalyst after longterm electrolysis were further investigated by LSV, XRD and XPS analyses before and after long-term electrolysis. First, the LSV curves of the Cu@nanosilica electrode showed only little decrease in current in the potential region of 1.5 V to 0.7 V for ECR, while the current for the Cu@nanosilica 1000 electrode after electrolysis decreased from 28 to 25 mA mg 1 in 1.5 V, as shown in Fig. S10. Second, the XRD pattern in Fig. S11 indicated that Cu@nanosilica catalyst remained almost the same before and after electrolysis. The overall structure of Cu@nanosilica 1000 also kept relatively stable after electrolysis (Fig. S12). Finally, the XPS study had also been employed to evaluate the variations of Cu chemical valences on the surface layer before and after the electrocatalysis processes (Fig. 4). In the Cu XPS regions, the characteristic peaks at 933.8 eV and 953 eV corresponding to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, respectively, and their shake-up satellite peaks, were clearly obtained. Combined with the peak of Auger Cu lmm region, the initial valance states of the Cu@nanosilica and Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalysts were determined as Cu2+ before electrocatalysis. After electrocatalysis, both the locations of Cu 2p3/2 and Auger Cu lmm peaks altered to the positions with lower binding energies, suggesting the existence of Cu+ (or Cu(0)) [15,17]. It was suggested before that the CO adsorption and dimerization would be enhanced when the Cu valence state was tuned between Cu(0) and Cu+ [2]. Both the Cu@nanosilica and Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalysts exhibited the same tendency, while their activity and stability differed a lot, suggesting their amorphous structure and urchin-like morphology played an important role in the ECR efficiency. Besides, these results also indicated that the Cu@nanosilica electrode/catalyst had high atomic/micro-scale structure stability. The final Cu/Cu+ moieties, rather than Cu2+ species, was responsible for the efficient ECR.
Association of thermo/kinetic changes of ECR with urchin-like structure and amorphous Cu dispersion facilitates in-depth under-
standing on the origin of excellent ECR activity/selectivity. Hence, double layer capacitance test, CO2 chemical desorption test and Tafel plot analysis were conducted. First, electrochemical surface area (ECSA) derived from double layer capacitance was calculated to be 9.77 cm2 mg 1 for the Cu@nanosilica catalyst, higher than that of the Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalyst (5.23 cm2 mg 1). This result is in highly agreement with the BET specific surface area measurement above. It represents more surface sites in the Cu@nanosilica (Figs. 5a and S13) compared to the Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalyst. When normalized to the ECSA, the ECR activity for C2H4 production on Cu@nanosilica is still higher than that on the Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalyst (see Fig. S14). It indicates the better
intrinsic activity of amorphous Cu catalyst compared to the crystalline counterpart. Second, CO2 adsorption on the surface Cu active sites is the first step for ECR, and the adsorption property was examined by CO2 temperature programmed desorption. As shown in Fig. S15, the Cu@nanosilica catalyst showed a clear peak centered at around 110 C, indicative of the CO2 adsorption on its surface. In contrast, the Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalyst did not show the corresponding peaks for CO2 desorption, probably because CO2 adsorption is very weak on its surface. This phenomenon evidenced that the amorphous Cu with higher coordinationunsaturated degree facilitated ECR via enhancing CO2 adsorption. Finally, the kinetic information for ECR to C2H4 on the catalysts was acquired by Tafel plot analysis. As seen in Fig. 5b, the Tafel slopes for the Cu@nanosilica catalyst was measured to be 145 mV dec 1, lower than that of the Cu@nanosilica 1000 catalyst (196 mV dec 1). According to the previously reported works [12,28,37–39] and this Tafel slope, the possible reaction steps leading to the formation of C2H4 have been proposed as below:

CO 2 þHþ ! COOH ð2Þ

(1)) [39]. CO2 * intermediate was then protonated to form CO* (Eqs. (2) and (3)), which is the pivotal intermediate to generate C2+ products (e.g. ethylene, ethanol, etc.) by C–C coupling (Eq. (4)). The lower Tafel slope of the Cu@nanosilica catalyst indicated the fast formation of these intermediates and their reactions during ECR. In general, the urchin-like Cu@nanosilica catalyst with amorphous Cu dispersion facilitated formation of CO2 * and possible CO* intermediates, acting as an important contributor for excellent ECR activity/selectivity.
Since urchin-like structure and amorphous Cu dispersion have endowed the Cu@nanosilica catalyst with excellent ECR efficiency; the catalyst was further equipped in two-electrode electrolyzer driven by potentiostat and solar cell for evaluating its practical applications. First, when powered by potentiostat (Fig. 6a), the electrolyzer had gained a current of 10.4 mA cm 2 at 2.9 V cell
voltage, with the cathode potential of 1.93 V vs. Ag/AgCl (with saturated KCl solution). Moreover, the FE for CO, CH4, HCOOH, C2H4, C2H5OH and C3H7OH was 20.5%, 2.5%, 16%, 40.5%, 7.5% and 5%, respectively (Fig. 6c). The H2 FE kept below 23% in all potentials and achieved only 18% at the cell voltage of 2.9 V (Fig. 6b), substantiating the domination of ECR processes on the cathode surface over a wide voltage range. The two-electrode electrolysis was performed several times, and the error scale in Fig. 6b and c demonstrated that the performance was repeatable. These results match well with the three-electrode tests.
When coupling with a commercially available polycrystalline Si solar cell (solar cell with short circuit current density of 5 mA cm 2, and open circuit potential of 2.0 V), the solar-driven electrolyzer can be built, with the configuration illustrated in Fig. S16. The Cu@nanosilica catalyst was used in the cathode and a Ru/C catalyst was used in the anode for oxygen evolution reaction. During 2.5 h electrolysis test (Fig. 6d), the current density of the electrolyzer kept at ca. 25 mA cm 2, and the cathode potential maintained at around 2.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl, demonstrating the overall good stability of the system. Fig. 6e showed that the C2H4 FE first increased, and then slightly decreased, which was mainly due to the increase of H2 production. The FE for H2, CO, CH4, HCOOH, C2H4, C2H5OH and C3H7OH at 1 h electrolysis was calculated to be 16.2%, 4.4%, 27%, 16%, 31%, 7.5% and 8.5%, respectively. Accordingly, the energy efficiency (EE) for C2+ products was calculated by the sum of that of C2H4, C2H5OH and C3H7OH, which was 20.0% at 1 h electrolysis (see supporting information). For the C1+ products, the EE even achieved 41.0%. These two EEs lead to the corresponding solarto-chemical efficiency (g) of 4% and 8% for C2+ and C1+ products, respectively. These solar-to-chemical efficiencies in solar-driven electrolyzer are comparable with or even better than the electrolysis systems reported by other works, as shown in Table S1. There still remains some room for improving solar-to-C2+ product efficiency in this system, and the effective strategy is to reduce the overpotentials of Cu@nanosilica catalysts for ECR.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we have synthesized amorphous urchin-like Cu@nanosilica hybrid via electrostatic coupling and hydrothermal processes. The amorphous urchin-like Cu@nanosilica electrocatalyst enabled efficient ECR to produce C2+ products with high FE of 70.5%, and higher ECR stability compared to the crystalline Cu counterpart. The solar-driven CO2 electrolysis also yielded a FE of 47% and energy efficiency of 20% for C2+ products. Mechanism study revealed that CO2 adsorption/activation to facilitate the generation of CO2 * and possible CO* intermediates was enhanced, while hydrogen evolution was suppressed concurrently, both making for efficient ECR.
